title: Jordan Zabrecky
text:
I am currently a PhD candidate in Natural Resources and Environmental Science at the University of Nevada, Reno in the Blaszczak Lab. Broadly, I am interested in the intersection of water quality, public & ecological health, and data science. My dissertation research focuses on understanding and forecasting the timing of toxin-producing cyanobacteria in rivers.
Outside of science, I am an avid rock climber. I also enjoy knitting, crocheting, and reading.

title: Understanding controls on growth and anatoxin production of benthic cyanobacteria
text:
overview
Cyanobacteria that grow attached to the bottom surface of aquatic environments (i.e., benthic cyanobacteria) can produce dangerous compounds known as anatoxins which have been responsible for the death of dogs in recreational areas. Unlike their free-floating counterparts (i.e., planktonic cyanobacteria) which often proliferate due to excess nutrients and high temperatures, benthic cyanobacteria are poorly understood. Often, benthic cyanobacteria are found in pristine, low nutrient rivers such as those in northern California that are popular recreational areas. Overall, this research aims to understand influences on benthic cyanobacteria growth and anatoxin production to better inform water recreation management.


















specifically, my research:

documents patterns of cover and anatoxin concentrations for two taxa of benthic cyanobacteria within three rivers and evaluates multiple covariates (e.g., temperature, nutrients, etc.) to predict future taxon-specific cover and anatoxin concentrations
characterizes changes in the surrounding algal and microbial assemblages of benthic cyanobacteria to identify potential species interactions that could influence or be related to anatoxin production






To do this work, I was fortunate to live at UC Berkeley’s Angelo Coast Reserve in northern California for two summers. Working out of the reserve, we (referring to myself and two helpful technicians!) sampled on the South Fork Eel, Russian, and Salmon Rivers (traditional homes of the Sinkyone, Pomo, and Karuk peoples respectively). All data collected are publicly released and can be found here.

















relevant publications

Kelly, L., S.A. Wood, [and 32 others including J.M. Zabrecky]. Tracking the global proliferation of benthic aquatic Microcoleus: taxonomy, distribution, toxin production, ecology, and future directions. Water Research. 249, 125441. DOI: 10.1016/j.watres.2026.125441

tl;dr- this is a review paper that highlights what we know about Microcoleus and highlights future research directions including prediction/forecasting and ecotoxological impacts!

Brown, S. M., J.R. Blaszczak, R.K. Shriver, R.C. Jones, A. Sohrab, R. Goel, G.L. Boyer, B.  Wei, K.M. Manoylov, T.R. Nelson, J.M. Zabrecky, and R. Stancheva. 2025. tl;dr- lab experiment showing that anatoxin production by Microcoleus is highest during the exponential growth phase and overall toxic strains had higher growth rates than nontoxic strains under luxurious nutrient conditions. this work used strains collected from the South Fork Eel River!

title: Predicting and forecasting cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (cHABs) in freshwaters
text:
overview
Cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (cHABs) can negatively impact water quality in quite a few ways such as the production of cyanotoxins and other nuisance compounds, reduction of water clarity, and creation of hypoxic (i.e., low oxygen) environments following their decay. Improving our ability to predict or forecast when cHABs will occur helps our ability to inform water quality management whether it be for drinking water or recreation. This research ties in both model development and ecological understanding to make better predictions and forecasts of cyanobacterial blooms.


specifically, my research:

tackles forecasting poorly-understood benthic cyanobacteria proliferations that grow on the bottoms of rivers by evaluating the potential of gross primary productivity (which reflects the activity of organisms undergoing photosynthesis in the river) as a predictor in addition to abiotic predictors (i.e., temperature, nutrients, discharge)

To estimate gross primary productivity (GPP) in rivers, we use high-frequency dissolved oxygen data collected from sensors. We then use that data with other data (such as temperature, light, river depth) to create time series estimates of GPP which we then compared to benthic cyanobacterial dynamics.
